solution:
Complete the hemisphere to a FULL spherical shell by adding its mirror image above the flat face. The field inside a complete uniform spherical shell is zero at every interior point, so at the centre the two half-shells must contribute equal and opposite fields.

Reflection in the flat face maps one half-shell onto the other. It reverses the component of a vector along the axis and preserves the components lying in the face, so if the lower half contributes \(\mathbf{E}\), the upper half contributes the reflected \(\mathbf{E}\). For the two to cancel, the in-plane components must each vanish, leaving a purely AXIAL field.

The shell's mass all lies below the flat face and gravity is attractive, so the intensity at the centre points vertically downwards, into the bowl — the straight-down arrow at the centre, drawn as \(c\) in Fig. 7.11.

Note the intensity is NOT zero here: only the complete shell gives zero, and half of it has been removed.

[Textbook cross-reference: this question opens "For the above problem" and is not self-contained as printed — it refers back to Exercise 7.10, which sets the same hollow hemispherical shell and the same lettered arrows in Fig. 7.11. The figure is attached above so the arrow directions can be read directly, and the answer below names the direction rather than relying on the cross-reference.] The same construction works at ANY point of the flat face, not only at the centre. Complete the hemisphere to a full spherical shell: the field vanishes everywhere inside a complete uniform shell, so at P the two half-shells contribute equal and opposite fields.

P lies ON the plane of reflection, so reflection in the flat face leaves P fixed while mapping one half-shell onto the other. That reflection reverses the axial component of the field and preserves the components lying in the face, so cancellation forces the in-plane components to vanish — even though P is off the axis.

The field at P is therefore purely axial, and since the mass lies below the face it points vertically downwards: the straight-down arrow at P, drawn as \(e\) in Fig. 7.11.

The arrows tilted out of the vertical, and the one lying in the plane of the face, are excluded precisely because the in-plane component must be zero.
